claimant_lives_in_uk.description: Whether the claimant lives in the UK.

children.description: A list of children the claimant is claiming for.

lives_with_claimant.description: Whether the child lives with the claimant.

in_approved_education.description: Whether the child is in approved education or training (e.g. A-levels, GCSEs, NVQ up to level 3). Only relevant for children aged 16-19.

in_extension_period.description: Whether the child (aged 16 or 17) has left education and registered with a government-sponsored careers service or the armed forces (qualifying for a 20-week extension).

upkeep_per_week.description: The amount in £ per week the claimant contributes towards the child's upkeep (food, clothes, pocket money, etc.). Only relevant if the child does not live with the claimant.

another_claimant_has_priority.description: Whether another person who also lives with the child has priority for claiming Child Benefit.

another_claimant_lives_with_child.description: Whether someone who lives with the child is already claiming Child Benefit for them.

care_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in local authority care.

care_home_24h_per_week.description: Whether the child spends at least 24 hours per week at home while in local authority care.

hospital_weeks.description: The number of weeks the child has been in hospital or residential accommodation.

claimant_spends_on_child.description: Whether the claimant regularly spends money on the child (e.g. food, clothes, books) while the child is in hospital or residential accommodation.

is_fostered.description: Whether the child is fostered by the claimant.

council_pays_for_child.description: Whether the local council pays towards the child's accommodation or maintenance.

works_24_plus_hours.description: Whether the child works 24 or more hours per week in paid employment.

started_apprenticeship_in_england.description: Whether the child has started an apprenticeship in England.

receives_qualifying_benefits.description: Whether the child receives qualifying benefits in their own right, such as Universal Credit or Employment and Support Allowance.

conversation.text: I'll help you determine if you're eligible for Child Benefit. Let me start the assessment process.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! Let's begin your Child Benefit eligibility assessment. 

First, I need to understand your situation regarding the child or children you're asking about:

**What is the age of the child you're claiming for?**

The age categories that matter are:
- **Under 16 years old**
- **16 to 19 years old**
- **20 years old or over**

Please let me know the age of your child (or children if you have multiple children you want to claim for).

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Hi, thanks for helping me with this. I'm asking about my son Alex - he's 17 years old.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Thank you for that information! So you're asking about your son Alex, who is 17 years old.

Since Alex is between 16 and 19 years old, I need to check some additional criteria. Let me navigate to the next step.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Perfect. Now, for 16-19 year olds like Alex, there are specific requirements. I need to know:

**Is Alex currently in approved education or training, or has he recently left education?**

Please tell me which applies:
1. **He is currently in approved education or training** (like A-levels, Scottish Highers, NVQs, or other approved programs)
2. **He has recently left approved education or training** (within the last 20 weeks)
3. **Neither** - he's not in education/training and hasn't recently left

Which situation describes Alex?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, he's currently studying - he's doing his A-levels at sixth form college.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Excellent! Since Alex is doing A-levels at sixth form college, he is in approved education. Let me check the education level requirements.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Great! A-levels are an approved (non-advanced) qualification for Child Benefit purposes. Now I need to check a few more details about Alex's education:

**Questions about Alex's A-level studies:**

1. **Is his course full-time?** (This means at least 12 hours per week of supervised study, which sixth form A-levels typically are)

2. **Is this education funded by an employer or linked to a guaranteed job with an employer?** (This would usually not apply to sixth form A-levels, but I need to confirm)

Could you confirm these details for me?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, it's full-time - he's there during the week like a normal school day. And no, it's not funded by an employer or anything like that - it's just regular sixth form.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Perfect! That's exactly what I needed to know. A-levels at sixth form college are approved education, and since it's full-time and not employer-funded, Alex meets the education requirements. Let me continue with the assessment.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
Good! Now I need to check Alex's work situation:

**Is Alex working less than 24 hours per week (or not in paid work at all)?**

For Child Benefit purposes, if a young person aged 16+ works 24 hours or more per week, they may not qualify. Does Alex work fewer than 24 hours per week, or is he not working at all?

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Well, he does work quite a bit actually - he has a part-time job at the supermarket and works full-time hours there alongside his studies.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I need to clarify this as it's important for the assessment. When you say he works "full-time hours" at the supermarket alongside his studies:

**Does Alex work 24 hours per week or more at the supermarket?**

For example:
- Working 3-4 hours after college several days a week plus a weekend shift might total around 15-20 hours per week (less than 24 hours)
- Working most evenings plus full weekend days might total 24+ hours per week

Could you tell me approximately how many hours per week Alex works at the supermarket? This is crucial because working 24 hours or more per week can affect eligibility, even if he's also in approved education.

conversation.author: actor
conversation.text: Yes, he works more than 24 hours a week - it's definitely full-time hours at the supermarket. I know it's a lot alongside his A-levels, but he manages both.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text: Thank you for clarifying that. Let me continue with the assessment based on this information.

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
I need to review this outcome more carefully, as the reason statement doesn't quite match Alex's situation. Let me gather the complete picture and provide you with a proper assessment.

Based on the information you've provided about Alex:
- He is 17 years old
- He is in approved full-time education (A-levels at sixth form college)
- He is also working 24+ hours per week at a supermarket

According to the Child Benefit rules, when a young person aged 16-19 is working 24 hours or more per week, this affects their eligibility for Child Benefit, even if they are also studying.

Let me provide you with the formal outcome:

conversation.author: eligibility_agent
conversation.text:
## Child Benefit Eligibility Assessment Result

**Result: INELIGIBLE**

I'm sorry, but based on the information you've provided, **you are not eligible for Child Benefit for Alex** at this time.

### Why Alex doesn't qualify:

While Alex is doing well by managing both his A-level studies and work, the Child Benefit rules state that young people aged 16 or over who work **24 or more hours per week are not eligible for Child Benefit**, even if they are also in approved education or training.

Alex meets the education requirements (A-levels are approved non-advanced education), but the fact that he works 24+ hours per week at the supermarket means he doesn't qualify under the current rules.

### What you can do:

- **If Alex's work hours reduce**: If Alex later reduces his work hours to less than 24 hours per week while continuing his studies, you may be able to claim Child Benefit again. You would need to notify HMRC of this change.

- **When Alex finishes work or education**: Keep track of any changes in his circumstances, as eligibility can change.

### More information:

For more details, you can visit: https://www.gov.uk/child-benefit/eligibility

I understand this might be disappointing news, especially as Alex is working hard at both his studies and his job. If you have any questions or if Alex's circumstances change, please don't hesitate to reach out.
